elements.id-string-3: The generalization problem on KBQA has drawn considerable attention.
elements.id-string-4: Existing research suffers from the generalization issue brought by the entanglement in the coarse-grained modeling of the logical expression, or inexecutability issues due to the fine-grained modeling of disconnected classes and relations in real KBs.
elements.id-string-5: We propose a Fine-to-Coarse Composition framework for KBQA (\model) to both ensure the generalization ability and executability of the logical expression.
elements.id-string-6: The main idea of \smodel is to extract relevant fine-grained knowledge components from KB and reformulate them into middle-grained knowledge pairs for generating the final logical expressions.\smodel derives new state-of-the-art performance on GrailQA and WebQSP, and runs 4 times faster than the baseline.Our code is now available at GitHub \url{https://github.com/RUCKBReasoning/FC-KBQA}.
elements.id-string-8: Question answering over knowledge bases (KBQA) aims to provide a user-friendly way to access large-scale knowledge bases (KBs) by natural language questions.
elements.id-string-9: Existing KBQA methods~\cite{ZHANG20231} can be roughly categorized into retrieval-based and semantic-parsing (SP) based methods.
elements.id-string-10: The former ~\cite{feng-etal-2021-pretraining-numerical,he2021improving,zhang2022subgraph} directly scores the relevance between the question and answer candidates, thus
elements.id-string-11: it is difficult to resolve the complex questions.
elements.id-string-12: On the contrary, some KBQA approaches, such as \cite{das2021case,kapanipathi2021leveraging,qiu2020stepwise,sun2020sparqa}, are based on semantic parsing (denoted as SP-based), which can address complex questions and achieve promising results on i.i.d.
elements.id-string-14: SP-based methods first translate the questions into logical expressions such as SPARQL and then execute them against KB to yield answers.
elements.id-string-15: As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:dataset}, a logical expression consists of multiple components such as classes and relations.
elements.id-string-16: Most existing SP-based approaches fail with logical expressions that contain unseen compositions of components (called compositional generalization) or unseen components (called zero-shot generalization).

elements.id-string-19: To address the above problem, GrailQA-Rank~\cite{gu2021beyond} proposes a BERT-based rank model to match the given question with each logical expression candidate, which leverages the generalization abilities of the pre-trained language models.
elements.id-string-20: On top of that, RNG-KBQA~\cite{ye2022rng} further uses a pre-trained generation model, which takes top-5 ranked logical expressions as the additional input beyond the question to generate the target logical expression.
elements.id-string-21: Behind these mainstream models, a logical expression is viewed as an inseparable unit during modeling.
elements.id-string-22: Actually, logical expressions are coarse-grained because they can be decomposed into relatively fine-grained components including relations, classes, entities, and logical skeletons (See examples in Figure~\ref{fig:KB}).
elements.id-string-23: Such coarse-grained modeling entangles representations of fine-grained components, thereby overfitting the seen compositions during the training process, which weakens the model's compositional generalization ability.
elements.id-string-24: Meanwhile, even though pre-trained language models can deal with zero-shot components to some extent, compositional overfit reduces their ability to identify individual unseen components with zero-shot generalization.
elements.id-string-25: To demonstrate the above idea, we perform a pilot study (Cf.
elements.id-string-26: the detailed settings in Section~\ref{sec:pre-experiment}) with two preliminary experiments: one calculates the similarity score between a question and each coarse-grained logical expression to obtain the most relevant one, and the other searches the most relevant fine-grained components to form the final logical expression of a question.
elements.id-string-27: We observe that \textbf{the fine-grained modeling derives more accurate logical expressions on both the compositional task and zero-shot task (Cf.
elements.id-string-29: It could be explained that fine-grained modeling focuses exclusively on each component, avoiding overfitting of seen compositions in the training data.
elements.id-string-30: Although some studies attempt to leverage fine-grained components, they only consider partial fine-grained components such as relations, classes, and entities ~\cite{chen-etal-2021-retrack}, or suffer from inexecutability due to disconnected fine-grained components in real KBs~\cite{shu2022tiara}.
elements.id-string-31: Thus, to both ensure the generalization ability and executability of logical expressions, we propose a \underline{F}ine-to-\underline{C}oarse composition framework for KBQA (\model), which contains three sub-modules.
elements.id-string-32: The overview of our model is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:over-view}.
elements.id-string-33: The first module is fine-grained component detection, which detects all kinds of fine-grained component candidates from Freebase by their semantic similarities with the question.
elements.id-string-34: Such component detection guarantees the generalization ability in both compositional and zero-shot tasks.
elements.id-string-35: The second module is the middle-grained component constraint, which efficiently prunes and composes the fine-grained component candidates by ensuring the components' connectivity in the KB.
elements.id-string-36: The final module is the coarse-grained component composition, which employs a seq-to-seq generation model to generate the executable coarse-grained logical expression.
elements.id-string-37: In addition to encode the fine-grained components, the middle-grained components are also encoded to enhance the model's reasoning capacity, so as to improve the executability of the generated logical expression.
elements.id-string-38: In contrast to previous work~\cite{cao-etal-2022-program,chen-etal-2021-retrack,shu2022tiara} that only uses the knowledge constraints to guide the decoding process, we emphasize injecting them into the encoding process, because the encoder which learns bidirectional context could better suit natural language understanding~\cite{du2022glm}.

elements.id-string-46: (1) We conduct a pilot study to reveal an intriguing phenomenon --- a fine-grained understanding of the logical expression helps enhance the generalization ability of SP-based KBQA methods, which is rarely discussed before.
elements.id-string-47: (2) We propose a fine-to-coarse composition framework \smodel to address the generalization problem, which takes advantage of the idea of fine-grained modeling.
elements.id-string-48: (3) We devise a middle-grained component constraint that is injected into both the encoder and the decoder to guide the seq-to-seq model in producing executable logical expressions.

elements.id-string-52: Many efforts are paid to solve generalization problems on SP-based KBQA.
elements.id-string-53: Some approaches, such as~\cite{lan2020query,gu2021beyond}, use a rank-based model that takes advantage of a coarse-level match between the question and the logical expressions or query graphs.
elements.id-string-54: They first enumerate numerous query graph candidates based on KBs and then they rank them according to how relevant they are to the question.
elements.id-string-55: Another line of approaches, in addition to the rank-based ones, makes use of a generation model.
elements.id-string-56: KQAPro~\cite{cao2022kqa} leverages BART to directly convert questions into logical expressions.
elements.id-string-57: Additionally, RNG-KBQA~\cite{ye2022rng} further injects top-k ranked logical expressions as an additional input to the question.
elements.id-string-58: CBR-KBQA~\cite{das2021case} injects analogous questions and their corresponding logical expressions from the training data to increase the generalization.
elements.id-string-59: All of the aforementioned methods are pure coarse-level frameworks that treat each coarse-grained logical expression as a separate unit.
elements.id-string-61: Many researchers have been motivated to address the generalization issue by the notion of utilizing decomposed components, such as class, relation, and logical skeleton.
elements.id-string-62: Some approaches~\cite{wang-etal-2020-rat,zhao-etal-2022-bridging,li2022resdsql} retrieve the relevant schema item such as relation and column as additional fine-grained input information, while another line of approaches~\cite{dong-lapata-2018-coarse} extracts the skeleton of logical expression as the decoder guide.
elements.id-string-63: Such methods primarily concentrate on the grammar of logical expression and often ignore the knowledge constraint, which is essential in large-scale KB.
elements.id-string-64: They usually focus on KBs or DBs that contain a small number of relations where a logical expression can be easy to be executable.
elements.id-string-65: Program Transfer~\cite{cao-etal-2022-program}, ReTrack~\cite{chen-etal-2021-retrack}, and TIARA~\cite{shu2022tiara} simply apply KB constraints to control the generation of the decoding process.
elements.id-string-66: As opposed to them, we make use of middle-grained KB constraints during both the encoding and the decoding processes to help the model better adapt to KB and ensure executability.
elements.id-string-69: A KB is comprised by ontology $\{(C \times R \times C)\}$ and  relational facts $\{(E \times R \times (E\cup C))\}$, where $R,C,$ and $E$ denote relation set, class set, and entity set respectively.
elements.id-string-70: Notably, we consider literal as a special type of entity.
elements.id-string-71: Specifically, an ontology triple $(c_d, r, c_r)$ consists of a relation $r \in R$, a domain class $c_d$ which denotes the class of the subject entities, and a range class $c_r$ which denotes the class of the object entities.
elements.id-string-72: Each class has multiple entities, thus an ontology triplet can be instantiated as several relational facts.
elements.id-string-73: For example, both $(e_1,r,e_2)$ and $(e_3,r,e_4)$ correspond to $(c_d, r, c_r)$, where $e_1, e_3 \in c_d$ and $e_2, e_4 \in c_r$.
elements.id-string-76: Given a natural question $q$, KBQA models aim to find a set of entities denoted by $A
elements.id-string-77: \subseteq E$ from KB as the answers to $q$.
elements.id-string-78: Instead of directly predicting $A$, SP-based KBQA models translate $q$ to an executable logical expression denoted by $s$ such as SPARQL, lambda-DCS~\cite{liang2013learning}, query graph~\cite{lan2020query}, and s-expression~\cite{gu2021beyond}.
elements.id-string-79: We select s-expression as our used logical expression since it could provide a good trade-off on compactness, compositionality, and readability~\cite{gu2021beyond}.
elements.id-string-80: The \textbf{logical skeleton} of an s-expression can be derived by removing all the relations, classes, and entities in the expression and only keeping function operators and parentheses.
elements.id-string-81: Specifically, we replace relations, classes, entities, literals with special tokens ``<rel>'', ``<class>'', ``<entity>'', ``<literal>'' respectively.
elements.id-string-82: Figure~\ref{fig:KB} shows an executable logical expression on the KB and its corresponding logical skeleton.
elements.id-string-83: We unitedly name the relations, classes, entities, and logical skeleton in an s-expression as the \textbf{fine-grained component}, while the complete s-expression is the \textbf{coarse-grained logical expression}.

The upper part of the subgraph illustrates examples of ontology triplets, while the bottom illustrates relational facts. }  \end{figure}
elements.id-string-88: In the step of fine-grained component detection, we perform class extraction, relation extraction, entity linking, and logical skeleton parsing to obtain the most relevant components of the question.
elements.id-string-89: Then we utilize the KB-based constraint to obtain middle-grained component pairs that are connected in the KB.
elements.id-string-90: Finally, a T5-based seq-to-seq model encodes the reformulated fine-grained and middle-grained candidates (reformulation unit), and employs a controllable decoder with dynamic vocabulary (control unit) to generate the executable target logical expression.}
elements.id-string-92: As analyzed in Section~\ref{sec:introduction}, considering the logical expression as a unit will lead to entangled representations of fine-grained components and thus weakens generalization ability.
elements.id-string-93: Here we study the necessity of fine-grained modeling by testing how coarse-grained and fine-grained matching methods perform when selecting a question's logical expression from the corresponding candidate pool.
elements.id-string-95: To simplify the experiment, we extract a toy dataset that only involves 1-hop logical expressions from GrailQA.
elements.id-string-96: Then, for the relation $r$ and the class $c$ in such logical expressions, we study the compositional generalization where the composition $(r,c)$ is unseen or zero-shot generalization where the individual $r$ or $c$ is unseen in the training data.
elements.id-string-97: For each question with its ground-truth logical expression, we select 100 logical expressions that share the same domain as the ground truth as the coarse-grained expression candidates.
elements.id-string-98: For fair comparison, we separate all of the relations, classes, and logical skeletons from the coarse-grained candidates as the fine-grained component candidates.
elements.id-string-100: We aim to find the target logical expression of a given question by a ranking model trained with a contrastive loss~\cite{chen2020simple}, which is also used by RNG-KBQA~\cite{ye2022rng}.
elements.id-string-101: The coarse-grained method concatenates a question and a candidate logical expression to feed into BERT, then the output embedding of [CLS] is fed into a linear layer to compute the similarity score.
elements.id-string-102: The fine-grained method follows the above pipeline, but the input is the concatenation of a question and a fine-grained candidate component, then scores each logical expression candidate by summing up the normalized question-component similarity scores.
elements.id-string-103: For both methods, we compute accuracy by evaluating whether the ground-truth logical expression owns the highest score in the candidate pool.
elements.id-string-104: \vpara{Observation --- Fine-grained modeling can better solve the generalization problems on KBQA.} The matching accuracy is reported in Figure~\ref{fig:pre_experiment}.
elements.id-string-105: The fine-grained method outperforms the coarse-grained method in both composition generalization and zero-shot generalization tasks.
elements.id-string-106: A possible explanation is the fine-grained matching focuses solely on each component and is simple to learn, which better capture the semantic information of each component and also well adaptable to express the various compositions of components.
elements.id-string-107: The coarse-grained matching, on the other hand,  attempts to describe all of the components as a whole composition, limiting the ability to express unseen compositions and components.
elements.id-string-108: Inspired by this, we propose \smodel in the next section.
elements.id-string-110: We propose a fine-to-coarse composition framework \smodel bridged by a middle-grained KB constraint.
elements.id-string-111: Figure~\ref{fig:over-view} illustrates the overall framework, which contains three parts:
elements.id-string-112: \vpara{Fine-grained Component Detection.} Given a question, we extract relation candidates and class candidates from the whole KB based on semantic similarity.
elements.id-string-113: Simultaneously, we adopt an entity linker to detect mentioned entities and use a seq-to-seq model to generate logical skeletons.
elements.id-string-115: Based on the detected components, we devise an efficient way to check the connectivity of component pairs on the KB, including class-relation pairs, relation-relation pairs, and relation-entity pairs.
elements.id-string-116: We only keep the executable component pairs to guarantee the executability of final logical expression.
elements.id-string-118: Finally, a seq-to-seq model takes the concatenation of the question and the reformulated components as input to generate the logical expression.
elements.id-string-119: In particular, the middel-grained components are injected into both the encoder and the decoder to ensure the executability of the final logical expressions.
elements.id-string-122: Taking the relation extractor as the example, given a question $q$, we aim to extract relations in $q$.
elements.id-string-123: First, we apply BM25~\cite{robertson2009probabilistic} to recall the relation candidates from the KB based on the surface overlaps between relations' names and $q$.
elements.id-string-124: Then we apply BERT~\cite{devlin2018bert} as the cross-encoder to measure the semantic similarity between $q$ and each relation candidate $r$.
elements.id-string-125: We describe $r$ using the relation domain, the relation name, and the relation range and let the BERT input be ``[CLS] q [D] domain(r) [N] name(r) [R] range(r) [SEP]'', where [CLS], [SEP], [D], [N], and [R] are the special tokens.
elements.id-string-126: To better distinguish the spurious relations, we sample the relations that share the same domain as the ground-truth relation as the negatives for training.
elements.id-string-127: The trained model is used to retrieve the set of top-$k$ relations, denoted by $R_q$.
elements.id-string-128: The class extractor works in the same way as the relation extractor.
elements.id-string-129: We represent the class using its name and domain, and use other classes in the same domain as negatives.
elements.id-string-130: $C_q$ represents the set of the top-$k$ relevant classes.
elements.id-string-132: A common paradigm of finding topic entities in KBQA methods is to first leverage a NER tool~\cite{finkel2005incorporating} to detect mentions and then apply an entity disambiguation model to link them to entities in KB.
elements.id-string-133: However, some noun-phrase mentions such as ``rich media'' are hard to be detected by the NER tool, and some ambiguous entities could not be distinguished by the pure entity names.
elements.id-string-134: To address both issues, we equip the NER tool\footnote{We follow GrailQA which utilizes an open BERT-NER tool on GitHub (https://github.com/kamalkraj/BERT-NER).} with a trie tree-based mention detection method and propose a relation-aware pruning method to filter the mentions.
elements.id-string-135: Specifically, we build a trie tree~\cite{fredkin1960trie} with the surface names of all entities in the KB.
elements.id-string-136: Then we can search noun phrase mentions in the question efficiently and link them to the KB by BLINK~\cite{wu2019zero} to obtain the corresponding entities $E_q$.
elements.id-string-137: After that, we propose a relation awared pruning strategy to prune $E_q$ by removing the entities that could not link to any relations in $R_q$.
elements.id-string-138: Finally, following GrailQA~\cite{gu2021beyond}, we choose the entity with the highest popularity.
elements.id-string-139: We define regular expressions to extract literals such as digits and years appearing in $q$.
elements.id-string-141: Logical skeleton parsing aims to transform a given question $q$ into a logical skeleton $l$.
elements.id-string-142: Because the logical skeleton is domain-independent, the parsing process could be generalized across domains.
elements.id-string-143: We adopt T5~\cite{raffel2020exploring}, a state-of-the-art generation model to parse logical skeletons.
elements.id-string-144: Since many entity names contain tokens such as ``and'' and
elements.id-string-145: ``of'' that may cause the logical skeleton to be incorrectly determined, we mask each mention $m \in M_q$ with the special token ``<entity0>'', ``<entity1>'', ..., in order of appearance.
elements.id-string-146: For example, we change ``Thomas was the designer of what ship?'' to ``<entity0> was the designer of what ship?''.
elements.id-string-147: We notice that a common error is parsing out logical skeleton with wrong relation numbers, for example ``<rel>'' instead of ``<rel><rel>''.
elements.id-string-148: Instead of increasing beam numbers, we manually add grammar rules, such as add ``<rel><rel>'' as the second candidate when ``<rel>'' is T5's top-1 prediction.
elements.id-string-149: The set of the top-2 logical skeleton candidates is denoted as $L_q$.
elements.id-string-151: After deriving the candidate components according to Section~\ref{sec:fine_grained},
elements.id-string-152: the KB-based constraint is required to guarantee the composed logical expression is executable.
elements.id-string-153: A straightforward idea is to fill the logical skeleton with candidate relations, classes, and entities, and execute them one by one to check executability.
elements.id-string-154: However, such enumeration is inefficient, since all combinations of candidate components should be considered.
elements.id-string-155: Therefore, we incorporate the middle-grained component pairs which are connected in KB.
elements.id-string-156: Such pairs can be produced efficiently to keep the model's efficiency.
elements.id-string-157: The middle-grained component pairs include class-relation pairs, relation-relation pairs, and relation-entity pairs.
elements.id-string-158: For each class $c \in C_q$ and each relation $r \in R_q$, if $r$ is connected with the domain class $c$, we add $(c, r)$ into the class-relation pair set $P_{c-r}$.
elements.id-string-159: For example in Figure~\ref{fig:KB}, the class ``railway.railway'' is linked with the relation ``rail.railway.terminuses'', so the pair (railway.railway, rail.railway.terminuses) is executable and will be added into $P_{c-r}$.
elements.id-string-160: If the range class of $r$ is $c$, we add the pair of $c$ and the reverse relation of $r$.
elements.id-string-161: We construct executable relation-relation pair set $P_{r-r}$ by checking each relation pair $(r_1\in R_q, r_2\in R_q)$.
elements.id-string-162: If $r_2$'s domain class does not match $r_1$'s range class, we directly remove this pair to maintain efficiency, otherwise, we reformulate $(r_1, r_2)$ to a logical expression and execute on KB to check its connectivity.
elements.id-string-163: For each relation-entity pair $(r, e)$, we first check whether the logical skeleton candidates contain the <entity> placeholder or not.
elements.id-string-164: If not, we leave $P_{r-e}$ empty; otherwise we directly take the result of the relation-pruning strategy for entities in Section~\ref{sec:fine_grained}.
elements.id-string-166: We apply a generation model based on T5 to compose all the above fine-grained and middle-grained component candidates and output an executable logical expression by a controlled decoder.
elements.id-string-168: Before feeding the fine-grained and middle-grained component candidates into the generator, we sort the middle-grained candidates according to their similarity scores to the question.
elements.id-string-169: By doing this, the order can reveal the pattern of which pair is more likely to appear in the ground-truth logical expression.
elements.id-string-170: In intuition, such a pattern will help to generate more accurate logical expressions.

elements.id-string-217: Both RNG-KBQA and GrailQA-Rank enumerate all the logical expressions in a 2-hop KB subgraph (enumeration), so it is time-consuming for the rank model to score thousands of logical expressions for each question (candidate selection).

elements.id-string-225: GrailQA does not provide ground truth for the test set, so we conduct the ablation studies on the public Grail-Dev to investigate how the fine- and middle-grained components affect the performance.
elements.id-string-226: As shown in Table~\ref{tb:ablation-result}, we develop four model variants.
elements.id-string-227: (1) \textbf{-Knowledge} removes all the fine-grained and middle-grained components except for the logical skeleton.
elements.id-string-228: (2) \textbf{-Knowledge Pairs} replaces the middle-grained components, such as  class-relation pairs and relation-relation pairs with the corresponding fine-grained candidates, such as classes and relations.
elements.id-string-229: (3) \textbf{-Logical Skeleton} gets rid of the logical skeleton.
elements.id-string-230: (4) \textbf{-Decode Constraint} deletes the dynamic vocabulary created with the middle-grained components.
elements.id-string-231: The results show that  removing ``knowledge'' reduces model performance by 60\% F1 score, and replacing  ``knowledge pairs'' with pure fine-grained components also reduces model performance by 28\% F1, indicating that encoding the middle-grained components can significantly improve the model's reasoning capacity.
elements.id-string-232: To further demonstrate that encoding such middle-grained components can also help improve other model's performance, we create Enhanced RNG-KBQA by taking the top-10 ranked results from its ranking model and formulating them into middle-grained component pairs to be injected into its encoder.
elements.id-string-233: The results in Table~\ref{tb:ablation-result} show that middle-grained reformulation improves the performance of RNG-KBQA.
elements.id-string-234: Middle-grained component pairs, like coarse-grained logical expressions, can guarantee connectivity, but they are more compact and much shorter.
elements.id-string-235: As a result, because PLMs have a maximum input length, the middle-grained formulation can inject more components and is more likely to cover the components involved in the target logical expression.
elements.id-string-236: Removing ``logical skeleton'' can result in a 3.0\% F1 drop, indicating that skeleton is useful for guiding the question understanding even though it is less important than the knowledge.
elements.id-string-237: Removing ``decode constraint'' in the decoder can also have an effect on model performance, but is much weaker than removing ``knowledge pairs'' in the encoder, indicating that injecting the knowledge constraints in the encoding process is more useful than in the decoding process, because the encoder learns the bidirectional context, which is better suited to natural language understanding.
elements.id-string-238: This is also a significant difference from the existing knowledge constrained decoding methods.
elements.id-string-239: Both "Knowledge Pairs" and "Decode Constraint" are proposed for addressing the in-executability issue, which guarantee all generated logical expressions are executable.
elements.id-string-240: Removing either reduces the accuracy, which indicates that high executability can improve the model performance.

elements.id-string-244: A typical mistake is on logical expressions that involve KB-specific component composition.
elements.id-string-245: For example, in Freebase, ``coach'' is represented by the join of ``sports.sports\_team.coaches'' and ``sports.sports\_team\_coach\_tenure.coach''.
elements.id-string-246: Our fine-to-coarse model only predicts the  previous relation but is unable to recall ``sports.sports\_team\_coach\_tenure.coach'', while some coarse-grained methods are able to memorize such composition and provide the correct answer.
elements.id-string-248: This paper proposes \model, a \underline{F}ine-to-\underline{C}oarse composition framework for KBQA.
elements.id-string-249: The core idea behind it is to solve the
elements.id-string-250: entanglement issue of mainstream coarse-grained modeling by the fine-grained modeling, and further improve the executability of logical expression by reformulating the fine-grained knowledge into middle-grained knowledge pairs.
elements.id-string-251: Benefiting from this, \smodel achieves new state-of-the-art performance and efficiency on the compositional and zero-shot generalization KBQA tasks.
elements.id-string-252: This fine-to-coarse framework with middle-grained knowledge injection could be inspiring for generalization on other NLP tasks.
elements.id-string-254: Although our model achieves good performance in solving the compositional and zero-shot generalization problems, there is still room for improvement on the i.i.d datasets.
elements.id-string-255: The fine-grained module in our framework cannot take advantage of explicit composition information when the component compositions in the testing set and training set significantly overlapp.
elements.id-string-256: For example, in Freebase, "Who is the coach of FC Barcelona?" is answered by the join of relation ``sports.sports\_team.coaches''
elements.id-string-258: Our fine-grained extractor may fail to recall ``sports.sports\_team\_coach\_tenure.coach'' and instead select ``base.american\_football.football\_coac-h.coach'' as the candidate  since `football coach'' is more relevant to the question than ``coach tenure'' in semantics.
elements.id-string-259: The only coarse-grained model, however, can directly memorize the pattern because such composition appears frequently in the training data.
elements.id-string-260: Therefore, compared to conventional models that completely memorize composition patterns, our model may only have minor advantages.
